1.title: Plan Mode, Iterative Refinement and CI/CD
1.text: Welcome to Module eight: Plan Mode, Iterative Refinement and C I C D. This module covers task statements three point four to three point six: plan mode, iterative refinement and c i c d. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Plan mode versus direct execution, and the Explore subagent. Four iterative refinement techniques: examples, test-driven iteration, the interview pattern, one message versus many. Running Claude Code in C I C D (continuous integration and continuous delivery): dash p, dash dash output format json, dash dash json schema, Claude dot M D for context, independent review, no duplicate comments.

1.title: Case Check-In: Two Tickets at Birchwood Supply
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Two Tickets at Birchwood Supply. Ticket A: "The checkout page crashes with a stack trace pointing to format Price when the price is null". Ticket B: "Replace the charting library in the reporting module; it touches more than forty files, and two candidate libraries need different hosting setups".

1.title: Plan Mode or Direct Execution
1.text: Plan Mode or Direct Execution. Plan mode lets Claude explore the code and design an approach without making changes. You review the plan, then approve it for execution. Choose it for. Plan mode: Complex tasks: large-scale changes, several valid approaches, architectural decisions, multi-file modifications (microservice restructuring, a library migration touching forty-five plus files, choosing between integration approaches with different infrastructure needs). Direct execution: Simple, well-scoped changes: a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace, adding one validation check. Benefit. Plan mode: Safe exploration and design before committing; avoids costly rework. Direct execution: Fast, no overhead. Wrong choice costs. Plan mode: Overhead for trivial work. Direct execution: Late discovery of dependencies and rework.

1.title: Plan Mode or Direct Execution, continued
1.text: Plan Mode or Direct Execution, continued. The figure shows this: Plan mode for complex, multi-file or architectural work; direct execution for small, well-understood changes; often plan first, then execute directly. Combine them: plan mode to investigate and plan (for example a library migration), then direct execution to carry out the chosen plan. Explore subagent: a built-in subagent that does verbose discovery work in its own context and returns a summary, so the main conversation does not fill up during multi-phase tasks.

1.title: Plan Mode or Direct Execution, continued
1.text: Plan Mode or Direct Execution, continued. If the complexity is already stated in the requirements (dozens of files, boundary decisions), start in plan mode; do not "see if it gets complicated". Enter plan mode with Shift plus Tab or claude dash dash permission mode plan; Claude reads and proposes a plan but makes no edits until you approve. Explore and Plan are built-in, read-only subagents. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: Complexity that is already stated in the requirements (dozens of files, several approaches) means plan mode now, not "switch if it gets hard".

1.title: Iterative Refinement
1.text: Iterative Refinement. Concrete input or output examples. Use it when: Prose descriptions are interpreted inconsistently. How: Give two to three examples of the input and the exact expected output. Test-driven iteration. Use it when: You can specify behavior as tests. How: Write the test suite first (expected behavior, edge cases, performance), then iterate by sharing test failures. Interview pattern. Use it when: The domain is unfamiliar or has hidden design choices. How: Have Claude ask you questions first (cache invalidation? failure modes?) before implementing. Specific test cases. Use it when: An edge case is mishandled (null values in a migration). How: Provide the case with example input and expected output.

1.title: Iterative Refinement, continued
1.text: Iterative Refinement, continued. One message versus several. Use it when: Problems interact. How: Put all interacting issues in one detailed message; fix independent problems one at a time.

1.title: Iterative Refinement, continued
1.text: Iterative Refinement, continued. The figure shows this: Five techniques for progressive improvement of results. Exam tip: Output formats keep coming back different from what you described? to show two to three concrete before or after examples, not a longer prose description.

1.title: Claude Code in CI/CD
1.text: Claude Code in C I C D. The figure shows this: In C I, run claude dash p so nothing waits for input, ask for Jason (Java Script Object Notation) that matches a schema, load standards from Claude dot M D, and post the findings as P R (pull request) comments.

1.title: Claude Code in CI/CD, continued
1.text: Claude Code in C I C D, continued. Run without interactive input (a plain claude "..." hangs waiting). dash p (or dash dash print): process the prompt, print the result, exit. Machine-readable results. dash dash output format json and dash dash json schema (structured findings to post as inline P R comments). Project context for C I runs. Claude dot M D: testing standards, fixture conventions, review criteria. Avoid duplicate comments after new commits. Include prior review findings in the context and tell Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues. Avoid duplicate test suggestions. Provide the existing test files in context. Better test generation. Document testing standards, what makes a valuable test, and available fixtures in Claude dot M D.

1.title: Claude Code in CI/CD, continued
1.text: Claude Code in C I C D, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Claude Code in CI/CD, continued
1.text: Claude Code in C I C D, continued. Independent review instance: the session that generated the code retains its reasoning, so it is less likely to question its own work. Use a second, independent Claude Code instance (no generator reasoning) to review. Distractors: there is no Claude H E A D L E S S environment variable and no dash dash batch flag for this purpose; redirecting stdin from or dev or null does not make Claude Code non-interactive.

1.title: Claude Code in CI/CD, continued
1.text: Claude Code in C I C D, continued. The structured result appears in the Jason output's structured output field (check it exists before using it). dash dash bare starts faster and is recommended for scripted calls, but it skips auto-discovery of Claude dot M D, hooks, skills and M C P (Model Context Protocol) servers: if you use it, pass context explicitly (for example dash dash append system prompt or dash dash mcp config). Add dash dash allowed Tools or a permission mode so no step waits for approval. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six. Exam tip: In C I always use dash p; for machine-readable output add dash dash output format json with dash dash json schema; give context through Claude dot M D.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Plan mode: Complex, multi-file, architectural, several valid approaches; explore and design before changing code. Direct execution: Simple, well-scoped (one-file fix with a stack trace). Both: Plan to investigate, then execute directly. Explore subagent: Verbose discovery in its own context; returns a summary. Refinement: two to three examples, tests first, interview first, specific edge cases, interacting issues together, independent ones in turn. C I flags: dash p or dash dash print (no hang), dash dash output format json, dash dash json schema. C I context: Claude dot M D (standards, fixtures, criteria); give prior findings and existing tests. Review: Use an independent instance; the generating session reviews itself poorly. Not real: Claude H E A D L E S S, dash dash batch.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Birchwood must replace the charting library in its reporting module. More than forty files are affected, and the two candidate libraries need different hosting setups. Which approach is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A multi-file change with several valid approaches and infrastructure consequences is what plan mode is for. Waiting for trouble ignores that the complexity is already known.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. A stack trace shows format Price crashing on a null price in one file. What is the best mode? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. A clear, single-file fix is well scoped; direct execution is efficient.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. During a multi-phase migration, discovery output (hundreds of lines of file listings) fills the main context. What helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery in its own context and returns only a summary.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A team describes a conversion rule in prose three times and Claude interprets it differently each time. What works best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Concrete input and output examples communicate the expected transformation unambiguously.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A developer needs a caching layer in an unfamiliar domain and does not know what could go wrong. Which technique brings up the unknowns? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Interviewing first surfaces considerations the developer had not thought of.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Three bugs in a pricing function interact (fixing one changes the others). How should they be reported? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Interacting problems should be addressed together; independent problems can be handled sequentially.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. A nightly job runs claude "Summarize today's failed tests" and never finishes because Claude Code waits for input. What is the correct change? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. dash p or dash dash print is the documented non-interactive mode for scripts and C I. Feeding fake input, hiding the terminal or waiting longer does not make the tool non-interactive.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. A C I job should post findings as inline comments through a script. What should the command output? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Machine-parseable structured findings that follow a schema are easy for a script to post as comments.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. After a developer pushes new commits, the review bot repeats comments already made. How can it avoid duplicates? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Prior findings in the context let Claude suppress what is already reported and mention only new items.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. Generated tests keep suggesting scenarios that already exist. Which change helps? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Showing the existing tests lets Claude avoid suggesting scenarios that are already covered.

2.title: Practice Question 11
2.text: Question eleven. The same Claude Code session that wrote a change is asked to review it and finds nothing. What is the better design? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The generating session keeps its reasoning and is less likely to challenge itself; independent review catches more.

2.title: Practice Question 12
2.text: Question twelve. Select two. Which two options help run Claude Code in a pipeline and return machine-parseable findings? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and D. dash p prevents waiting for input, and the Jason options give structured output. The other options are not the documented mechanism.

2.title: Practice Question 13
2.text: Question thirteen. Select two. Which two tasks favor plan mode? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. Large multi-file changes and architectural choices benefit from planning before editing. Tiny, well-scoped edits are quicker with direct execution.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all thirteen answers. Question one: D. Question two: B. Question three: B. Question four: D. Question five: C. Question six: A. Question seven: C. Question eight: D. Question nine: D. Question ten: B. Question eleven: A. Question twelve: A and D. Question thirteen: B and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
